newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian shares retreat, BUX futures follow suit.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian shares retreat, BUX futures follow suit.

text.p: The Hungarian share market closed lower on Wednesday, reflecting a global negative sentiment, a weaker dollar and recent disappointing corporate earnings, market participants said.
The BUX index finished at 7,816.26 points, down 142.87 points or 1.80 percent.
"It's a reflection of world markets and overall sensitivity to what's going on Wall Street," said Tom Chadwick, Vice President for Emerging Markets Europe at Merrill Lynch.
BUX futures closed lower for all maturities.

"The (futures) market started with an early clearing for December," said Peter Lencs of MKB Securities. "Sentiment was so pessimistic because of the dollar's (weak) level and SEAQ prices that many expected serious falls."
A weaker dollar makes the forint, thus Hungarian shares more expensive for foreigners.
Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs) of Hungarian companies opened weaker on the SEAQ where trading starts before the opening of share trade on the Budapest bourse.
In late futures trading the nearer maturities fell, while long-term ones remained fairly steady. December BUX ended at 8,515 points, down 160.

The forint strengthened against the dollar, and stood at 198.28/33 at midday, compared with 198.40/45, but was steady against the central bank's dollar/mark basket and remained at its resistance level.
Chadwick said that recent disappointing first half results by pharmaceuticals Egis, hotel firm Danubius and to a lesser extent meat processor Pick, weighed on spot prices.
"There have been a number of disappointing results that have come out in the last couple of days that haven't been quite as strong as maybe people were hoping for," he said.
Egis has continued to decline since the first half figures were published on Monday. On Wednesday it finished at 11,025 forints, down 610. Danubius ended at 6,400, up 10 and Pick at 15,200, down 505.
However, results by some companies like home improvement product maker Graboplast pleased investors.
"I see a clear link between Graboplast's earnings and the rise in its shares," Tamas Revesz of Wintrust said earlier, adding the group's earnings were above expectations.
Chadwick added that people are now beginning to look at Poland. "It is now beginning to look like the fourth quarter might start to see a revival of the Polish equity market."
